Participants also completed two tests of working memory, a collection of four subtests of low-level visual perception ability, and three tests used as indicators of g.

To examine whether the perception and memory type o tests measure separable abilities we compared a model with a single o factor to one that had separate Op and Om factors. To examine whether Op and Om factors differentially measured perception and memory, we tested whether a low-level visual perception factor predicted Op and whether a working memory factor predicted Om. To examine whether any residual covariance between Op and Om could be explained by g, we controlled for g in addition to low-level perception and working memory, and tested whether Op and Om had a significant residual correlation.

Method Participants

Participants were recruited online on the Prolific.com platform. Participants had to reside within the US, age between 18 and 45 years, report fluency in English, have normal or corrected-tonormal vision, and have a > 95% approval rating for previous studies. We preregistered that we would collect data from 350 participants. A total of 351 participants began session one, of whom 346 completed at least one task and 298 completed session two. Preregistered exclusion criteria specified that participants who performed below chance on more than one test would be excluded. This criterion is based on tasks for which chance performance can be clearly calculated (i.e. not time-limited tasks that include Raven's Matrices and Number Sequences, and not Operation Span where chance is complicated to compute). This led to the exclusion of 23 participants, leaving a final sample of 275 (125 men, 147 women, 1 refused to say, 1 selected "other"; Mage = 32.5, SD = 7.0) who completed all tasks. The data were collected between the 12 th August and the 2 nd September 2024. This study received ethical approval from the Vanderbilt University Institutional Review Board (#222116). We report how we determined our sample size, all data exclusions (if any), all manipulations, and all measures in the study.

Tests

Object Recognition -Perception (Op)

These tasks required recognition of complex objects that shared a common configuration of features with the distractor items (Figure 1). These tasks make strong perceptual demands: objects are visually similar and some tasks have limited encoding times and visual noise. None of these tasks require memorization of objects for longer than a second and two of the tasks rely on judgments of simultaneously presented stimuli. While three of these tests have been used to measure o previously, Silhouette Matching is newly developed.

Many Objects Oddball

On each of 45 trials, a fixation cross (250 ms) was followed by an array of three objects from a single novel object category (presentation times ranged from 750 to 4000 ms across trials). Two objects shared an identity but differed in size and orientation, while the other object had a unique identity. After the objects disappeared, empty squares appeared in the spatial locations in which the objects had appeared. Unlimited time was given to select the square in the location where the odd-one-out object had appeared. After an answer choice was selected, feedback appeared for 1000 ms. Novel object categories changed from trial to trial. Some objects appeared with visual noise. Further test details can be found in Smithson et al. (2024).

Silhouette Matching

On each of 40 trials a target object appeared at the top of the display, while an array of three silhouettes simultaneously appeared below. One silhouette matched the target object while the other two silhouettes were distractors. The silhouettes sometimes appeared in a different viewpoint from the orientation of the target object. Unlimited time was given to select the silhouette that matched the target. The novel objects used were YUFOs -a type of computergenerated novel object discriminable only by subtle differences in shape (Gauthier et al., 2003).

Ensemble Perception -Transformers

Ensemble perception requires judgments about the summary statistics of groups of objects.

Although we do not aim to measure ensemble perception as a construct here, this task also relies on object recognition for accurate performance and thus can serve as a measure of object recognition when combined with other object recognition tasks in a model. This task and similar ones have been used successfully as indicators of o in prior work (Chang et al., 2024; Sunday et al., 2022). On each of 50 trials, an array of four Transformer robots appeared for 1000 ms. After a 1000 ms interstimulus interval, an array of six Transformer morphs appeared. Participants had to select the morph that was closest to the average of the four study Transformers. Performance was indicated by absolute error in degrees within a circular morph space. There were four initial practice trials with feedback. Chance performance was 90°. For details of the morphing procedure, see Chang & Gauthier (2022). For further task details, see Chang et al. (2024).

Three-Alternative Forced-Choice Matching Task -Asymmetrical Greebles (3AFC Ma)

Each of 51 trials began with a fixation cross (500 ms) before a target object appeared. This was followed by a mask of scrambled object parts presented in visual noise (500 ms), and finally an array of three test objects. One test object matched the target object, while the other two test objects were distractors. Participants had unlimited time to click on the object that matched the target. Three initial trials were followed by four blocks consisting of 12 trials each. Blocks one, two, three, and four had target object presentation times of 300 ms, 500 ms, 750 ms, and 1000 ms respectively. In block one the targets appeared in the same orientation across study and test. In block two the targets appeared in different orientations across study and test. In block three the targets appeared in the same orientation across study and test but appeared with added visual noise during study. In block four, the targets appeared in different orientations across study and test but with added visual noise during study. The orientation changes were horizontal rotations of approximately 30°. The objects were Asymmetrical Greebles -a type of computer-generated novel object (Richler et al., 2017). Further task details can be found in Smithson et al. (2024).

Object Recognition -Memory (Om)

These tasks required recognition of complex objects (Figure 2). The tasks required encoding several similar objects and maintenance of this information in memory across more than a few seconds. While Learning Exemplars has been used to measure o previously, Paired Objects, New Object, and Recognition Memory are newly developed.

Learning Exemplars -Vertical Ziggerins (LE)

Six Vertical Ziggerins, a type of novel object (Wong et al., 2009), appeared simultaneously for 20 s. Participants were instructed to memorize these targets. This memorization phase was followed by six test trials, another memorization phase of 20 s, 18 test trials, a final memorization phase of 20 s, and 24 more test trials. Each test trial required selecting which object from an array of three matched one of the six memorized targets. The "g", "h", and "j" keys were used to indicate the leftmost, middle, and rightmost object respectively. Further details can be found in Smithson et al. (2024).

Paired Objects

Participants were asked to memorize five pairs of objects. Each pair consisted of one Ziggerin (Wong et al., 2009) and one abstract 2D shape (Lindell et al., 2022). To begin, each pair of objects was displayed onscreen for four seconds before memory for that pair was immediately tested. In these tests each 2D shape appeared next to a question mark and participants clicked on which of an array of three Ziggerins completed the pair. Each trial ended with feedback (500 ms). This block was followed by five test trials, in which each pair was tested once.

Subsequently, the pairs were again serially presented for study (4000 ms each). This study block was followed by another block of ten test trials. For these trials there was no feedback, and the last five of these trials displayed three distractor Ziggerins next to the correct answer, rather than two distractors like in previous trials. This was done to increase difficulty. Finally, there were 15 more test trials in a different format. In these trials, two object pairs were presented and participants had to click on the one pair that was correct, no feedback was given. There were 35 test trials in total.

New Object

An array of three novel objects (Quaddles; Watson et al., 2019) appeared for 3000 ms. This was followed by 44 trials. On each trial, four Quaddles appeared. Three of the Quaddles had appeared before while one was always novel. The task was to click on the Quaddle that had never appeared before. Feedback appeared for 1000 ms after each of the first five trials. There was a 500 ms interval between each trial.

Recognition Memory

This test began with a study phase. Participants studied sets of target objects. Each set contained four objects from one of from six categories (a total of 24 objects). The sets were very distinct from one other, and the sets varied in the extent to which objects within the set differed from one another. All objects within a set were presented simultaneously and each set was presented for 15 s. After the study phase participants read a short story and answered a basic reading comprehension question. Following this delay, there were 24 test trials in which memory for each of the target objects was tested. On each trial, one of the target objects appeared in an array alongside two distractor objects from the same object category. Stimuli were obtained from multiple sources (Behrmann & Williams, 2007; Cooper et al., 2023; firstpalette.com, 2024; Horst & Hout, 2016; Leek et al., 2012; Richler et al., 2019).

Working Memory (WM)

These two tests were developed by Chow et al. (2023) and were based on tests from Wilhelm et al. (2013). The two tests were chosen to tap different aspects of working memory: Verbal-Numerical Binding requires forming and retaining arbitrary associations between elements, whereas Operation Span requires maintaining items across an unrelated processing task (Wilhelm et al., 2013).

Verbal-Numerical Binding

On each of the first 15 trials, participants were presented with a sequence of word-number pairs. Each pair appeared for 2000 ms and there was an interstimulus interval of 1000 ms. After each sequence, participants were shown either a word or a number that appeared in one of the pairs in that sequence and had to click which number or word correctly paired with it. The answer options consisted of either all of the numbers or all of the words that were presented in the sequence. The sequences ranged from two to six word-number pairs and the test was not speeded. On an additional two trials, every word in that trial's sequence was individually probed, and each correct number appeared among two distractors from previous trials. Each participant had to make 27 responses in total.

Operation Span

On each of 15 trials, participants had to remember a sequence of letters while performing an arithmetic distraction task. On each trial, letters and simple arithmetic statements were presented in an alternating sequence. For each arithmetic statement participants could click "Correct" or "Incorrect" to indicate whether the displayed answer was correct. The arithmetic statements appeared for 3000 ms, or less if a response was made. Letters appeared for 1000 ms each. At the end of every sequence, participants were asked to type the correct sequence of letters. Trials were scored according to the proportion of letters correctly remembered in the correct positions in the sequence. The letters were all consonants and half of the arithmetic statements were correct.

Low-Level Visual Discrimination: Hanover Early Vision Assessment (HEVA)

The HEVA battery (Kieseler et al., 2022) measures perceptual discrimination ability for basic visual features. On each trial, three images appeared for 1500 ms, two of which were the same, and one of which was different. Participants indicated which image was the odd one out by pressing "f" (leftmost image), "space" (central image), or "j" (rightmost image) on their keyboard. There were 96 trials in total, with 16 blocks of six trials each. Each block used images that displayed variations of a single feature type (distance between dots, circle size, angle size, and line length). We did not include the ellipsoid size trials that are ordinarily included in this battery as this could be considered a mid-level feature. The first eight blocks were administered in session one, the last eight blocks were administered in session two. Each session contained two blocks for each feature type to reduce the impact of session-related variance.foot_0

General Ability (g)

Matrix reasoning, number series, and vocabulary tests were chosen as indicators of g, because they have been shown to have sizeable g loadings (Gignac, 2015). Additionally, the non-g variance in each test is not likely to be shared between them as they are also measures of different broad abilities.

Raven's Matrices

On each of 18 trials, participants were given a 3-by-3 matrix of symbols with the bottom-right symbol missing. Using the number keys (1-8), participants had to select which one of eight possible answers would correctly complete the pattern. There were three practice trials with feedback and explanations. Participants had 10 minutes to complete as many of the 18 trials as possible.

Number Series

On each trial, a sequence of numbers appeared above five possible answer choices. The task was to select the number that came next in the sequence. After three practice trials with feedback and explanations, participants had five minutes to complete as many of 15 trials as possible.

Vocabulary

On each of 30 trials, a word appeared above an array of three possible synonyms that served as answer options. The task was to select the answer which was most semantically similar to the word. This task was based on a test from Warrington et al. (1998), but we added an additional choice for each trial.

Procedure

The study spanned two sessions. Task order was fixed across participants to minimize variance not associated with individual differences (Goodhew & Edwards, 2019). Indicators for each construct were spread across both sessions to minimize any effect of session-related variance on inter-construct relationships. In session one, participants completed the following tasks in order: Many Objects Oddball (Op), Ensemble Perception (Op), Paired Objects (Om), New Object (Om), Verbal-Numerical Binding (working memory), Raven's (g), Hanover Early Vision Assessment -1 st half (low-level visual discrimination). In the second session participants completed the following tasks in order: 3AFC Matching (Op), Operation Span (working memory), Learning Exemplars (Om), Silhouettes (Op), Number Series (g), Recognition Memory (Om), Hanover Early Vision Assessment -2nd half (low-level visual discrimination), Vocabulary (g). The median time to complete session one was 40.9 minutes, the median time to complete session 2 was 43.4 minutes. We embedded 18 simple attention checks across the tasks, but we did not preregister any exclusions on this basis. These attention checks were extremely easy versions of trials such that only inattentive responders would select the wrong answer (e.g. distractor items are from an extremely different category of objects from the target).

Transparency and Openness

All data, analysis code, and output are available at https://osf.io/d7cp4. This study was preregistered at https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/AFDB8. Code and materials for the object recognition tests are available at https://github.com/OPLabVanderbilt/Ojs.

Results

Descriptive statistics and reliability are shown in Table 1. Correlations between all tests are shown in Table 2. Test scores were of acceptable reliability. Almost all tests correlated positively with one another, as is expected of cognitive ability tests. All within-construct correlations were positive. (Callender & Osburn, 1979). Time is the median number of minutes taken, * indicates time limits for the Raven's Matrices and Number Series tasks. For low-level visual discrimination tests, median time is provided for the overall test combined across both sessions. SEM analyses were conducted using the lavaan package in R (Rosseel, 2012). As a Henze-Zirkler (Henze & Zirkler, 1990) test indicated that the joint distribution of the 19 tests was not multivariate normal (HZ = 1.004, p < .001), we conducted all SEM analyses using maximum likelihood estimation with robust standard errors and a Satorra-Bentler scaled test statistic (Satorra & Bentler, 1994). Model fit was assessed using several measures. The chi-square test of exact fit assesses whether the model-implied covariance matrix exactly matches the population covariance matrix. If the test is significant, this suggests that the model does not fit perfectly.

However, as all models can be expected to have at least minor misspecifications, this test is often significant at moderate or large sample sizes even for well-fitting models. Consequently, model fit is typically assessed using other fit indices. The Comparative Fit Index (CFI) ranges from 0 to 1, with greater values indicating superior fit. It assesses the relative fit of the model compared to a baseline model where all covariances are set to 0. Values > .95 are often taken to indicate acceptable fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999). The root mean-squared error of approximation (RMSEA) reflects the discrepancy between the model-implied and observed covariance matrices while penalizing model complexity (defined as the number of parameters estimated by a given model). Superior fit is indicated by smaller values, with those <.06 often considered to suggest close fit (Hu & Bentler, 1999). CFI and RMSEA were corrected for nonnormality using the method described by Savalei (2018).

Comparisons were made using three approaches. The chi-square difference test compares the goodness-of-fit chi square value of a model that is nested within a less restrictive model. The more restrictive model can be transformed into the less restricted model by removing constraints on parameters. The scaled-difference test was used to correct for nonnormality (Satorra & Bentler, 2001). A significant result indicates that the constraints in the more restricted model impaired model fit. Models were also compared on criteria that penalize model complexity. The Bayesian Information Criterion (BIC; Schwarz, 1978) and the Akaike Information Criterion (AIC; Akaike, 1974) were used to compare models, with lower values indicating superior fit.

Object Perception and Object Memory

In this preregistered model (Model 1, Figure 3), we included only Op and Om tests to assess whether these are separable constructs. Op and Om factors were only allowed to explain variance in their respective indicators and these two factors were allowed to freely covary. All tests loaded significantly onto their respective factors. All errors were specified to be independent. We preregistered a test of a modification allowing Paired Objects and Learning Exemplars to have correlated errors due to their shared use of the Ziggerin object category.

However, this modification did not significantly improve model fit (Δχ 2 (1) = 0.0586, p = .81) and the correlated error was not significant (r = .02, p = .81). We therefore treated these errors as independent in this and all further models. Op and Om were strongly correlated (r = .79, 95% CI [.68, .90]), but separable. We compared this two-factor model with one where a single o factor explained variance in all o tests. This is equivalent to setting the correlation between the two factors to r = 1. The one-factor model fit substantially worse than the two-factor model (Model 2, Table 3). Both AIC and BIC also favored the two-factor model, strongly suggesting that the Op and Om factors differ from one another. Note. Standardized solution. All paths are significant with p < .05. See Table 3 for fit statistics. Note. χ 2 test of exact fit uses the Satorra-Bentler scaled test statistic (Satorra & Bentler, 1994). Δχ 2 test of a difference in fit is scaled according to Satorra & Bentler (2001). Nonnormality-corrected RMSEA and CFI were calculated according to the method in Savalei (2018).

Conditioning on Working Memory and Low-Level Discrimination

In this preregistered model (Model 3a, Figure 4) we conditioned Op and Om on low-level visual discrimination and working memory. This allowed us to ask to what extent Op and Om can be differentially explained by these abilities. In this, and all further models, we parceled (Little et al., 2013) the two working memory tests into four indicators in line with our preregistration.

This design decision was made as a precaution because factors with two indicators are locally under-identified and often lead to improper solutions (Little et al., 2002).

Low-level visual discrimination significantly predicted both Op and Om, but the relationship with Op was much larger than the relationship with Om. Working memory significantly predicted Om, but did not significantly predict Op. This pattern of results accords with the view that Op tests differ from Om tests because they differentially tap into perceptual and memory abilities. The residual correlation between Op and Om was very strong (r = .94, 95% CI [.47, 1.41]) suggesting that the remaining variance in Op and Om is nearly completely shared. Note. Standardized solution. Bolded paths are significant with p <.05. Scaled χ 2 (96) = 137.53, p This can be especially problematic when the parameter value is close to the boundary. Two alternative methods of calculating the CI avoid the symmetry issue -likelihood ratio confidence intervals and bootstrapped confidence intervals. We were unable to calculate robust likelihoodbased CIs using the R package, semlbci (S. F. Cheung & Pesigan, 2023). However, semlbci does not support the necessary adjustment for bounded parameters in cases where the value is close to the parameter boundary (Wu & Neale, 2012). To obtain corrected values, we refit the model using the R package OpenMx (Neale et al., 2016) which provides an implementation of this correction (Pritikin et al., 2017). We obtained all the same model parameter estimates as in lavaan, however, the CI was again incomputable. Bootstrapping results from lavaan were also unsatisfactory, returning an impossible estimate of the upper CI after 10000 samples (r = .95, 95% CI [0.57, 2.48]). We found that 3986 of the 10000 bootstrap samples returned inadmissible model solutions, while 803 failed or did not converge. In 3887 of the inadmissible solutions, the parameter estimate for the correlation between Op and Om was greater than one. The large number of inadmissible solutions in this case may simply reflect sampling variability around a population parameter that is near its boundary and does not necessarily suggest that the model is incorrect (Chen et al., 2001; Van Driel, 1978). However, our results encouraged us to explore alternative models.

One possible issue is that our two working memory tests do not measure a unitary construct. They correlated only .24 to .27 and they showed inconsistent patterns of correlation with the other variables (Table 2). This is what would be expected if the two tests index distinct facets of working memory (Wilhelm et al., 2013), and it suggests that modeling them as separate factors may be a more appropriate specification. In an exploratory analysis we modeled two separate working memory factors -operation span and binding. Each working memory factor had two parceled indicators, with each indicator consisting of scores for one half of the trials, which were split into alternating halves. This model (Model 3b, see supplementary materials) fit significantly better than the model with a single working memory factor (χ 2 (2) = 7.30, p = .026) and was favored by AIC, although not by BIC. The correlation between Op and Om remained high (r =.76, 95% CI [.52, 1.00]) and had an admissible CI. Both the binding (.41) and operation span (.20) working memory factors significantly predicted Om, each making an independent contribution. Both binding (.14) and operation span (-.09) memory factors did not significantly predict Op. As in Model 3a, low-level visual perception significantly predicted Op (.76) and Om (.39). Again, the results were in line with our expectations that Om would be predicted by working memory ability, that Op would be predicted by low-level visual perception, and that there would be a strong residual correlation between Op and Om.

Conditioning on Working Memory, Low-Level Discrimination, and g

In this preregistered model (Model 4a, Figure 5), we asked whether the residual relationship between Op and Om found in Model 3a after conditioning on working memory and low-level visual discrimination could be explained by a shared relationship with g. To do this we added g as a predictor into the structural model. Supporting the view that the relationship between Op and Om cannot be entirely explained by g, there was a strong residual correlation (r = .84, 95% CI [.06, 1.51]). When this model was compared with one where the correlation between Op and Om was fixed to zero (Model 5a, Table 4), model fit was significantly impaired in the constrained model. These results indicate that Op and Om share variance that cannot be explained by lowlevel perception, working memory, or g. Op was significantly predicted by low-level visual discrimination (.48) and g (.53), while Om was significantly predicted by working memory (.56) and g (.51). A Wald test (Klopp, 2020) found that the standardized path from working memory to Om was significantly greater than the standardized path from working memory to Op (diff = 0.62, W(1) = 18.11, p < .001). The opposite pattern was true for the predictive effect of low-level visual perception (diff = 0.45, W(1) = 15.30, p < .001). These results align with the view that Op and Om differentially tap into perception and memory abilities, whereas both Op and Om tap into general cognitive ability. As was the case for the models without g, the solution was admissible, but the upper bound of the CI for the correlation between Op and Om was an impossible value (1.51). We therefore conducted an exploratory analysis of a model with separate binding and operation span memory factors (Model 4b, Table 4, see supplementary materials) instead of a unitary working memory factor. This model fit significantly better than the model with a single working memory factor (χ 2 (3) = 9.28, p = .026) and was favored by AIC but not by BIC. The results agreed with those of Model 4a. Both the binding and operation span memory factors made significant independent contributions to Om, while Op and Om retained a substantial and significant residual correlation (r = .59, 95% CI [.19, .99]). Unlike Model 4a, this interval did not extend beyond the parameter boundary. When this model was compared with another model with two working memory factors but where the correlation between Op and Om was fixed to zero (Model 5b, Table 4), the model with the constraint on the correlation fit significantly worse (χ 2 (1) = 5.84, p = .016).

While the results from the preregistered analyses were in line with our predictions, we conducted an additional non-preregistered analysis to obtain a more precise estimate of the residual correlation between Op and Om. Our preregistered approach used participants with complete data only. However, missing data techniques can be employed to include the full sample. Models 4a and 4b were refit to data from all 346 participants who completed at least one task, using maximum likelihood to deal with missingness (Enders & Bandalos, 2001; see supplementary materials for model results). Model 4a retained a strong residual correlation between Op and Om (r = .85, 95% CI [0.26, 1.45], as did model 4b (r = .70, 95% CI [.37, 1.03]).

This evidence strongly suggests that Op and Om retain substantial covariance after controlling for the other abilities.

Higher-Order o

In a non-preregistered model (Model 6, Figure 6), we explored the extent to which Op and Om could be explained by a higher-order o factor. If o tests that challenge perception measure both o and low-level visual perceptual ability, and if o tests that challenge memory measure both o and memory, then the Op and Om subfactors ought to load substantially onto a single o factor, plus either perceptual ability or working memory ability respectively. In this model, g is allowed to predict o, working memory, and low-level visual discrimination, while o, working memory, and low-level visual discrimination are allowed to predict Op and Om. While Model 4 represented the o-specific variance that is shared between Op and Om as a residual correlation which we interpret as evidence of a shared reliance on o, this model explicitly models an o factor as the cause of this shared variance. This model is a reconceptualization rather than an independent test of our main hypothesis. It provides a way of assessing the relationship between o and g. The model had good fit (Figure 6), and the results accorded with expectations.

Both Op (.68, 95% CI [.44, .92]) and Om (.63 [95% CI [.34, .89]) loaded substantially onto the higher-order o, and the remaining variance in each subfactor could be explained by either working memory or low-level perceptual ability. Ninety-five percent of Op variance could be explained, with higher-order o and low-level visual discrimination as the only significant predictors, while 99% of Om variance could be explained, with higher-order o and working memory as the only significant predictors. The higher-order o factor loaded substantially (.80) onto g, which could explain most of the variance in o. However, a substantial amount of o variance remained unexplained (37%).

Discussion

Our results confirm the notion that perceptual type o tests and memory type o tests measure separable Op and Om abilities (Model 1, Figure 3). As predicted, Op had a strong relationship with low-level visual discrimination ability, while Om had a strong relationship with working memory (Model 3a, Figure 4). Importantly, the remaining variance in Op and Om was largely shared between them. This residual covariance was not simply explained by g, as the Op and Om residuals remained strongly related even after controlling for g (Model 4a; Figure 5). When we modeled Op and Om as subfactors of a higher-order o in an exploratory analysis, they both load substantially onto it, in addition to low-level visual discrimination or working memory respectively (Model 6, Figure 6). This accords with our view that tests that challenge object perception and tests that challenge object memory can both measure a general object recognition ability but additionally measure either perceptual or memory abilities.

O in Relation to g and Other Abilities

While Models 4 & 6 suggest that o cannot be explained only by g, these two abilities are clearly strongly related (r = .80 in Model 6). This is line with prior findings that a visual o factor correlated r = .70 with g, and that an o factor that generalized across visual and auditory domains correlated r = .80 with g (Smithson et al., 2026). While o tests may appear quite distinct from the tests of fluid reasoning that are most closely associated with g, these results are consistent with hierarchical theories of cognitive abilities such as the Cattell-Horn-Carroll model (Schneider & McGrew, 2018; Smithson & Gauthier, 2026).

As the ability being measured becomes more general, the expected relationship with g becomes stronger. Any individual recognition test using a specific stimulus category may be expected to correlate only weakly with g, while factors that explain covariance among multiple tests that use the same category can be expected to correlate more moderately with g. Meta-analytic estimates, corrected for unreliability, place the correlation with intelligence at .42 for face perception tests and .26 for face memory tests (Walker et al., 2023). A factor explaining covariance among multiple tests that use multiple categories should be much closer to g, as is the case for o. In comparison, a broader ability than o should correlate more strongly with g, as is found for general visual processing, which often correlates greater than .90 with g (Caemmerer et al., 2020; Horn & Stankov, 1982; Keith & Reynolds, 2018; Smithson et al., 2026). While the o and g relationship was strong, we were still able to observe substantial variance that was specific to o (37%).

To provide an interesting contrast, whether a set of correlated factors reflects a common ability after accounting for general abilities was recently investigated for executive functions, with a different result. Segura et al. (2026) regressed three intercorrelated executive factors on a factor built from the low-demand control conditions of the same tasks, finding that the executive factors retained little residual variance and that their intercorrelations, the empirical basis of executive "unity," became largely nonsignificant. The residual correlation between Op and Om behaves differently, surviving control for low-level discrimination, working memory, and g. That most of the variance in o tests is shared with more general abilities is therefore not evidence against o, the relevant question is whether specific variance remains, and here it does.

However, it remains possible that the residual covariance between Op and Om reflects contributions to both types of task from an ability other than a domain-general high-level encoding ability. Shared task demands that are not relevant to o are a possible alternative explanation for the residual relationship.

Our results suggest that Om specifically relates to working memory capacity, while Op has no unique relationship with it. The tasks we chose to use, Operation Span and Binding measure general rather than visual working memory, and they index distinct facets of it (Wilhelm et al., 2013). It is possible that a visual working memory factor would have more of a relationship with both Om and Op. While prior work suggests that visual short-term memory can only explain a small proportion of variance in o (Chang & Gauthier, 2021; Richler et al., 2019), it may be fruitful for future work to investigate this possibility at a larger scale. Likewise, Op related to low-level visual discrimination, whereas Om had no unique relationship with it.

Implications for measuring o Smithson et al. (2024) suggested that a set of three tests could adequately measure o. These tests -3AFC Matching, Many Objects Oddball, and Learning Exemplars -were included in the battery of o tests in the present study. Importantly, these three tests were originally created to differentially make demands on perception and memory, and as such, their shared variance ought to reflect an o factor that is common to both perceptual and memory o tests. The present results support the rationale behind selecting these three tests: because Op and Om are separable, a battery that samples both types is needed to isolate what is common to them. Our models suggest that if one is interested in measuring o, and not perception or memory specifically, it is necessary to combine perceptual type and memory type tests. The present results suggest that this trio of tests remains adequate to measure o.

However, the results also suggest that this trio may not be the optimal selection of tests.

Learning Exemplars had the lowest loading onto Om of the four Om tests, suggesting that the other newly created Om tasks are likely to be superior. It is therefore suggested that researchers wishing to measure o with a small number of measures should favor New Object or Recognition Memory over Learning Exemplars due to their higher factor loadings and the high reliability of these tests in our sample. Because Op and Om are separable, an equally weighted composite will reflect whichever test type is more numerous. Prior work has used two perceptual tests and one memory test, tilting the composite toward Op. Researchers forming such a composite should use equal numbers of perceptual and memory type tests. While our work addresses the principal two axes by which object recognition tests can be organized -perception and memory, further divisions could be made. For example, the role of task demands on perceptual speed has been suggested as an area that future work should investigate (Smithson & Gauthier, 2026).

The majority of variance in all the o tests used in this study was not related to o. Future studies could modify these tasks to obtain higher reliabilities. This would likely allow for higher factor loadings and thereby produce tighter bounds on estimates of correlations among factors.

The moderately sized factor loadings we obtained are likely to have contributed to imprecision in the estimate of the residual correlation in the present results. While object recognition ability can be reliably measured by combining o tests, it is a greater challenge to reliably measure the portion of o that is independent of other abilities. In the psychometric literature, specific abilities are the portion of an ability that is left after accounting for g (Coyle & Greiff, 2023).

While often overlooked, the challenge of reliably measuring specific abilities is formidable, and psychometric batteries of cognitive abilities that are designed to measure specific abilities often fail to reliably do so (Canivez & Youngstrom, 2019). The same issue applies to o tests, as a majority of the variance they capture is shared with other abilities that may contribute to object recognition. Many domain-general perceptual and cognitive processes are involved in recognizing objects, so this result should not be surprising. For similar reasons, the issue affects tests of many other constructs like spatial ability (Lohman, 1996; Smithson et al., 2026), working memory (Colom et al., 2004; Conway et al., 2003; Kyllonen & Christal, 1990) or verbal ability (Carroll, 1993).

The difficulty of reliably measuring the portion of o that is independent of other abilities poses a challenge for research investigating hypotheses that are specific to o. One possible solution may be to explore other measurement approaches. Fast Periodic Visual Stimulation (Norcia et al., 2015) is an EEG approach that has been successfully used to reliably measure the ability to individuate faces (Rossion et al., 2020) without the need for a behavioral task. There is already evidence for neural correlates of o expressed broadly in extrastriate areas with fMRIadaptation, when participants are not trying to discriminate or memorize objects (McGugin et al., 2023). It may be possible to use such neural measures to measure other high-level visual abilities (Sigurdardottir et al., 2021), including o, without relying on psychometric tasks that are necessarily multifactorial.

Implications for Domain-Specific Abilities

Our research using non-face object stimuli has implications for research into domain-specific abilities. For example, face recognition and face perception are often considered to be distinct (Stantić et al., 2023; Walker et al., 2023; Wilhelm et al., 2010). The present finding that Op and Om are separable abilities raises questions about findings obtained with face stimuli. While face perception and face memory factors were separable in prior research (Wilhelm et al., 2010), it is unclear whether they would remain distinct after controlling for Op and Om. While Wilhelm et al. (2010) did control for an object cognition factor -measured by a set of object recognition and perception tasks -they did not attempt to control for object perception and object memory separately. Consequently, their results suggest that there are individual differences in face processing that are specific to faces (after controlling for an o-like factor), but they could not determine whether the distinction between perception and memory abilities with faces is specific to faces.

In our view, individual differences with any particular category will become more domain specific as experience with that category becomes more varied (Smithson & Gauthier, 2026; Sunday et al., 2019). As domain-general object perception and memory are distinct, we would expect that a distinction between perception and memory abilities could be found with all object categories. A distinction that is specific to a particular category (e.g. faces) might only arise if some individual differences in experience with that category are associated uniquely with either perception or memory. Future research could assess whether training on a specific stimulus category using only perceptual type tasks or only memory type tasks causes transfer learning from one task type to the other.

High Versus Low-Level Visual Perceptual Abilities

Our results suggest that the ability to discriminate visual stimuli along a single low-level feature dimension, as measured by HEVA, predicts the ability to discriminate complex objects along multiple feature dimensions simultaneously (Op). However, these two abilities appear quite separable, with the low-level discrimination ability only moderately uniquely predicting Op ( = .48, Model 4, Figure 4). This result accords with a prior study in which overall scores on the HEVA battery correlated only moderately with aggregate o scores (r = .45, r = .50 when disattenuated for measurement error; Smithson et al., 2024). A direct comparison can also be made between HEVA and Many Objects Oddball, as both tasks have a similar format, requiring participants to detect the odd one out among simultaneously presented stimuli. The difference between them is that Many Objects Oddball uses complex objects that vary on multiple feature dimensions. Smithson et al. (2024) obtained a small-to-moderate correlation between these tasks (r = .24, r = .31 disattenuated). A somewhat larger relationship is obtained if the same analysis is performed with the present data (r = .46, r = .58 disattenuated), but the abilities remain clearly separable. This distinction between high-level and low-level individual differences may not apply across all kinds of visual abilities -for example, individual differences in the ability to accurately estimate summary statistics for groups of visual stimuli do not differ across low and high-level visual properties (Chang et al., 2024).

Conclusion

Our results suggest that separable domain-general object perception and memory abilities can be measured by object recognition tasks that stress perception or stress memory respectively.

However, both types of tasks appear to tap into a common domain-general object recognition factor, which cannot be explained only by general cognitive ability.
